function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
**Artificial Intelligence (AI)** is the field of computer science that focuses on creating systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence. These tasks include reasoning, learning, perception, language understanding, problem‑solving, and decision making. | Aspect | What it means | |--------|---------------| | **Core Idea** | Machines that can *think* or *act* like humans, or at least emulate certain aspects of human cognition. | | **Key Capabilities** | • **Learning** – acquiring knowledge from data (machine learning, deep learning).
• **Reasoning** – drawing conclusions, planning, solving puzzles.
• **Perception** – interpreting sensory input (vision, speech, touch).
• **Language** – understanding and generating natural language. | | **Types** | • **Narrow/Weak AI** – specialized for one task (e.g., image recognition, chess).
• **General/Strong AI** – would possess full human‑level intelligence (still theoretical). | | **Historical Milestones** | • 1950s – Turing Test, early symbolic AI.
• 1960s‑70s – expert systems, rule‑based reasoning.
• 1980s – neural networks revival.
• 2000s – big data & GPU‑accelerated deep learning.
• 2010s‑present – breakthroughs in vision, NLP, reinforcement learning. | | **Common Techniques** | • **Symbolic AI** – logic, rules, knowledge graphs.
• **Machine Learning** – supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement.
• **Deep Learning** – neural nets with many layers (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers). | | **Applications** | • **Healthcare** – diagnostics, drug discovery.
• **Finance** – fraud detection, algorithmic trading.
• **Transportation** – autonomous vehicles.
• **Customer Service** – chatbots, recommendation engines.
• **Creative Arts** – music composition, image generation. | | **Ethical & Societal Issues** | • Bias & fairness.
• Privacy & surveillance.
• Job displacement.
• Accountability & explainability. | In short, AI is about building intelligent agents—software or hardware—that can learn from experience, adapt to new situations, and perform complex tasks, often surpassing human performance in specific domains.
